title: Dhritarashtra's Blind Love
text:
Dhritarashtra, the blind king of the Kurus, loved his eldest son Duryodhana beyond reason. When the boy was born, there were terrible omens, and the king's wise half brother Vidura advised him to give up the child for the sake of the family. Dhritarashtra could not do it.

As Duryodhana grew up, his jealousy of his cousins, the five Pandava brothers, grew with him. He tried to poison Bhima and later to burn all the Pandavas alive in a house built of lacquer. Each time Dhritarashtra was told, and each time he found reasons not to act.

When Duryodhana schemed to win the Pandavas' kingdom through a rigged game of dice, Vidura begged the king to stop it. Gandhari, Duryodhana's own mother, urged him to restrain their son. Dhritarashtra agreed that it was wrong, then allowed it anyway, because he could not bear to refuse his son. The Pandavas lost everything, and their wife Draupadi was dragged before the court and humiliated.

Years later, when Krishna came to negotiate peace, Duryodhana refused to give the Pandavas even five villages. Dhritarashtra again failed to overrule him. The great war at Kurukshetra followed, and all of Dhritarashtra's hundred sons were killed.
lesson: Loving a child sometimes means saying no and enforcing it. A parent who cannot refuse a favorite child can let a small fault grow into a disaster for everyone.
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sabha Parva and Udyoga Parva
